author: Thomas Hardy
title: Poems of the Past and the Present
edition: Poems of the Past and the Present, the second collection in the combined Macmillan pocket volume (London: Macmillan and Co., 1919, a reprint of the first pocket edition of June 1907), as transcribed by Project Gutenberg (eBook 3168); the collection was first published in 1901 (dated 1902). The volume’s first collection, Wessex Poems and Other Verses, is held separately as hardy-wessex-poems-1919. The library holds every poem in printed order under the five part titles, with Hardy’s three footnotes; the transcription’s underscore emphasis, curly quotation marks and display capitals stand. “The Darkling Thrush” was collated on 2026-11-18 against the OCR of Internet Archive wessexpoemsother00hardiala (the same pocket edition, 1907 setting, reprinted 1908) and against its page images for pp. 399–400 (p. 401 by OCR only): the transcription agrees with the print in every word and point.

rights.basis: Poems of the Past and the Present was first published in 1901 (dated 1902), and this text in the Macmillan edition of 1919; both were published before 1931, and their US copyright terms have expired. Project Gutenberg identifies this transcription as public domain in the USA.

acquisition.method: Project Gutenberg 3168 plain text (UTF-8) from the PG mirror aleph.pglaf.org. Took the text from “V.R. 1819–1901” after the contents up to PG’s FOOTNOTES list; the PG header and footer, the cover picture, title page, copyright leaf and contents were dropped, and a level-1 title heading supplied. The five part titles are level-1 headings; poem titles with their subtitle lines are level-2 headings (lines joined by line breaks), and roman section numbers level-3 headings; stanzas keep their lines with the common indentation removed and inner indentation kept; place and date lines, scene directions and lone parenthesised form labels such as (TRIOLET) are paragraphs, with lines joined by single spaces. PG’s page-numbered note anchors {253}, {290} and {457} became [1], [2] and [3], and each note a paragraph [Footnote n: …] after the poem that holds its anchor.
